**The organising principle:** one geographic cluster per day, so you never cross the city between meals. Sightseeing is placed in the same district as that day's food, and each day has only two or three eating events — Korean portions are large, and market snacking fills you faster than people expect.

**The week (written to start on a Saturday):**

| Day | Cluster | Food anchor |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Sat | Jongno / Gwangjang | Gwangjang Market: bindaetteok, mayak gimbap |
| 2 Sun | Mapo: Mangwon, Yeonnam | Cooking class, then Mangwon Market + river picnic |
| 3 Mon | Noryangjin / Yeouido | Buy-and-cook fish market lunch |
| 4 Tue | Seochon → Euljiro | Tongin brass-coin lunchbox; Nogari Alley at night |
| 5 Wed | Bukchon, Insadong, Ikseon-dong | Temple cuisine lunch; dakhanmari dinner |
| 6 Thu | Seongsu / Ttukseom | Gamjatang; craft makgeolli evening |
| 7 Fri | Namsan / Jangchung-dong | Jokbal street; barbecue finale |

**The reason the days are in that order** is the closure pattern, which is what quietly wrecks most Seoul food itineraries. Tongin Market shuts Mondays *and* the third Sunday of the month, Gyeongbokgung closes Tuesdays, Changdeokgung closes Mondays, and Balwoo Gongyang (the temple-cuisine restaurant) closes Sundays. So Monday is given to Noryangjin, which trades 24 hours year-round; Tuesday uses Deoksugung instead of Gyeongbokgung; and the temple lunch sits on a Wednesday. If your arrival day differs, rotate whole days rather than reshuffling — the notes in the document explain why, and there's a closure quick-reference at the end.

Two things worth flagging: only five items actually need booking (listed as a checklist), so the week stays flexible; and the distinctive experiences are spread one per day rather than clustered — the cooking class is deliberately on Day 2, early, because it makes everything you eat afterwards more legible.
